name: Sam Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior administrator at a housing association's regional office, so about forty staff and a few thousand tenants. I get in at half eight, open the post, and sort the repair requests, the tenancy paperwork and the diaries for the housing officers. I run the paper filing room too, and I'm proud that I can put my hand on any tenancy file in under a minute. What wears me out is the phone: tenants who've been passed around five times end up with me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fixing the knots nobody else can. Last week an older tenant, Mr Adeyemi, had his boiler repair booked three times and cancelled three times because the system kept losing it. I walked the job sheet over to the contractor myself, and the boiler was fixed by Friday. That's the bit of the job I'd miss if it went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone at our place got excited about the new software last year and it mostly made more forms. I'd tell my mates the tenants still need someone who picks up the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit wary. Even a small bit of automation could be the excuse management use to not replace Joyce when she retires, and then her work lands on me. Our budget's been squeezed for three years running, so the cuts don't need AI to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep my head down. I'd keep paying into my savings, about two hundred a month, because our rent went up again in September. I'd also push at the union branch meeting to make sure any new system comes with a promise on staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, but not relaxed. The rent and the budget squeeze were there before any of this AI talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cuts don't need AI. What's the pressure that's already there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association lost part of its grant last spring, so every vacancy now has to be signed off by the director. We've already lost one housing officer post and nobody replaced her. I end up covering bits of her paperwork on top of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your partner do if the rent goes up again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Dara and I already talked about it over dinner. We'd stay put for another year and cut the takeaways and the car, since we barely use it. Moving is its own cost and I don't fancy the hassle.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** mostly gave us more forms, not less work.
Tenants still need a **real person** who answers the phone and follows things through.
think: Even small automation could be an **excuse** not to replace staff who retire.
Our **budget squeeze** started years ago, so the pressure is there with or without AI.
do: Keep **saving** about two hundred a month despite the September rent rise.
Raise **staffing promises** at the next union branch meeting before any new system arrives.
feel: Relieved the big change didn't come, but still **uneasy** about money and the office budget.
S0.quote: I'd tell my mates the tenants still need someone who picks up the phone.
fieldNote: He sees the **real threat** as funding cuts, not technology, and AI Plateau doesn't touch that.
His pride in the **paper filing room** is personal; it's part of how he sees himself.
He's already **covering** an unfilled post, which keeps him on edge even in the mildest picture.

steps.text: Keep the two hundred a month going into savings
Ask the union branch for staffing promises on any new system
Sell the car and cut takeaways if rent rises again

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this needs rules. If software is going to book repairs and answer tenants, there should be a law that a human checks it. I'd probably share stuff from the union about it online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this one is aimed straight at me. Booking, filing, answering the same five questions from tenants, that's most of my week. I'm the senior one, so maybe I'm the last to go, but there'd be fewer of us and I don't use any of these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union first and get us a seat at the table when the new system comes in. I'd stick another three hundred a month into savings, which means no holiday this year. And I'd probably, grudgingly, sit the training they offer, because if I refuse it I'm the obvious one to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really. I'm good at a job that might be shrinking under me, and I'm the one who hasn't kept up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI tools. What would it take for you to try one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone at work showing me it doesn't lose things. My worry is a tenant's complaint vanishing into a chatbot and nobody knowing. If it keeps a proper trail I'd use it, but I'd hate every minute at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joyce, who's fifty-nine and does the rent arrears letters. She's brilliant on the phone but she'd struggle with a new system even more than me. I'd want the union to make sure people like Joyce get proper time to learn.

say: I'd say software that books repairs needs a **law** making a human check it.
I'd share the **union's** line online that tenants deserve a person, not a chatbot.
think: Booking, filing and answering tenants is **most of my week**, so this picture is aimed at me.
Being senior might keep me longer, but there'd be **fewer of us** and I've no AI skills.
do: Get the **union** a seat at the table when the new system arrives.
Put an extra **three hundred** a month into savings and skip this year's holiday.
Sit the employer's **training**, grudgingly, so I'm not the obvious one to cut.
feel: **Anxious** that a job he's good at is shrinking under him.
Embarrassed that he's the one who **hasn't kept up**.
S1.quote: If software is going to book repairs and answer tenants, there should be a law that a human checks it.
fieldNote: His first move is always **collective**: the union before himself.
He'll learn the tools only out of **fear of being cut**, not curiosity.
His worry for an older colleague shows how much he values **fairness** at work.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a seat on the new system's rollout
Add three hundred a month to savings and skip the holiday
Sit the employer's AI training course even though he dislikes it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say government has to step in now, with income support and a pause on mass layoffs, because two years is nothing. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd write to our local MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job is gone by 2028. Everything I do is paperwork and screens, and a robot doesn't even need to come for me, the thinking AI does it all. The three-year gap before robots only helps people who work with their hands, and that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking straight away at something hands-on, maybe a maintenance apprenticeship with the association's repairs team, because they'd have until 2031. Dara and I would put off any talk of buying a flat. Every spare penny would go into savings, and I'd sign every petition going for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'd be lying awake doing sums about how long three months of savings lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said every spare penny goes into savings. What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, the streaming, the weekend trips to see Dara's family by train. We'd stop eating out completely. It'd stretch the savings to maybe five months, not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the repairs team rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know the lads there and I know the work they do, every job sheet goes through me. I'm not handy now, but I'd rather learn plumbing at twenty-eight than sit at home. At least the robots are three years behind the software.

say: I'd demand government **income support** and a pause on mass layoffs straight away.
I'd go to every **union meeting** and write to our local MP.
think: My **paperwork job** is gone by 2028, because thinking AI covers all of it.
The **three-year gap** before robots only helps people who work with their hands.
do: Apply for a **maintenance apprenticeship** with the association's repairs team.
Shelve talk of **buying a flat** with Dara and save every spare penny.
Cut the gym, streaming and **train trips** to stretch savings to about five months.
feel: **Sick** with worry and lying awake doing sums about his **savings**.
S2.quote: I'd rather learn plumbing at twenty-eight than sit at home.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that his work is **all thinking work**, so the robot delay doesn't help him.
For someone who resists change, the jump to an **apprenticeship** shows real fear.
He still reaches for **politics and the union** before his own plan.

steps.text: Apply to the association's repairs team as a maintenance apprentice
Put off buying a flat with Dara
Cancel the gym, streaming and weekend train trips
Write to the local MP about income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but with more time to organise. I'd say we've got five years to get proper rules in place, so let's not waste them. I'd want every housing association to sign a deal on retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't change the end for my job. It just means a slower slide, with fewer staff each year and me doing more. I'm not good with change, and I know I'd be tempted to wait until it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year to decide, which is hard for me. I'd look at the social housing officer route, because that's dealing with people in crisis, and at the repairs apprenticeship. I'd keep saving the extra three hundred a month and push the union for retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like a deadline I can see but can't make myself move towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the housing officer route? That's partly paperwork too.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, and the paperwork side would go. But the bit where you sit in someone's kitchen while they cry about arrears, I don't see software doing that by 2031. I'd want the part of the job that's people, not forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be tempted to wait. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dara, probably. She'd keep asking me at dinner what I'd done about it that week, and she wouldn't let it drop. I need someone pushing me, I know that about myself.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get proper rules in place and shouldn't waste them.
I'd want every housing association to sign a **retraining deal**.
think: Five years means a **slower slide** for my job, not a different ending.
I'm **not good with change**, so I'd be tempted to wait too long.
do: Set a **one-year deadline** to choose between housing officer work and the repairs apprenticeship.
Keep the extra **three hundred** a month going into savings.
Push the union for **retraining money** from the association.
feel: A **heavy** feeling, like a deadline he can see but **can't move** towards.
S3.quote: I'm not good with change, and I know I'd be tempted to wait until it's too late.
fieldNote: He's honest that his **resistance** to change is his biggest risk.
He looks for the **human part** of nearby jobs, the kitchen-table moments.
His partner Dara acts as his **push**; he relies on her to keep him moving.

steps.text: Choose within a year between housing officer work and the repairs apprenticeship
Keep saving the extra three hundred a month
Ask the union to win retraining money from the association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly if government actually plans for it. I'd be pushing for free retraining and a shorter working week. I'd sound calmer, but I'd be saying the same things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years gives me a real chance. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which is young enough to have a whole second career. My job still goes, but I'd have time to move without panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time housing studies course at the college next September, evenings, which the association sometimes pays for. I'd keep saving but not as hard, and Dara and I might still try to buy a small flat in the next few years. I'd stay active in the union, because the rules matter even with time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then a bit more hopeful. A decade is long enough that even someone slow like me can move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI tools in your current job, given ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once they're boring and everybody uses them. I'd let Joyce's replacement, whoever that is, show me. I won't be the first, I never am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend starting out in admin now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to build their whole career on filing and booking. Learn the people side, the bit where someone's upset and you sort it out. Paperwork skills like mine have a shelf life.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if government actually plans for it.
I'd push for **free retraining** and a shorter working week.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd still have time for a whole second career.
My job still goes, but I could **move without panicking**.
do: Start a part-time **housing studies** course at the college next September.
Keep saving more gently and still consider **buying a flat** with Dara.
Stay active in the **union** to shape the rules.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, then more **hopeful** that even he can move in time.
S4.quote: Paperwork skills like mine have a shelf life.
fieldNote: Time turns his **dread** into a plan he can follow at his own pace.
He still expects to **lose this job**, so the worry doesn't go away.
He's frank that he'll adopt AI **last**, once it's boring.

steps.text: Enrol on an evening housing studies course next September
Keep going to union meetings to shape the rules
Keep saving steadily while looking at a small flat with Dara

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years is nothing when your whole job is paperwork and you've never touched these tools. What would help is proper income support while people retrain, and an employer that pays for apprenticeships instead of just letting people go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's going to look after the tenants. Everyone talks about the jobs, but the people we house are the ones who'll be stuck talking to a machine about a broken boiler. I worry about them as much as me. And for me, I can put my hand on any tenancy file in under a minute, and nobody will care about that skill in five years.

headlineQuote: I can put my hand on any tenancy file in under a minute, and nobody will care about that skill in five years.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old** senior administrator at a housing association, proud of his **paper filing room**.
He's **progressive** and reaches for the **union** and government rules before his own plan.
He's **resistant** to new tech and has **never used** AI tools.
He moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** under fast AGI, eased only by ten years' warning.
His partner **Dara** keeps him moving, and he worries for **tenants** as much as himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job is all **paperwork** and he has no AI skills.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** while people retrain, and employers paying for **apprenticeships** instead of layoffs.
